title: High-performance computing
outline: Lecture 15 video (Data Science, COM3021): High-performance computing (title card "HPC clusters"). 11 scenes, 132 s, from videos/_plan/ds-15-script.md. Running example: Priya (Gullhaven Sailing Club) borrows the university cluster Kestrel (8 nodes: cpu n1-n6, gpu n7-n8) for her storm model; job 4021. Colour roles: blue compute, purple communication, orange I/O and waiting, red limits, green results, grey machines and frames.

title: Three days on a laptop,
so borrow a cluster
caps: On a laptop, the storm model takes 3 days.
Three things make a system fast: processing, communication, I/O.
One giant machine, or many computers on a network.
A cluster has nodes; nodes hold processors; processors hold cores.
4 × 2 × 8 = 64 cores working at once.

title: Speed is counted
in sums per second
caps: One sum on decimal numbers is a floating-point operation.
FLOPS: how many of them a machine does per second.
Giga, tera, peta, exa: each rung is 1000 times the last.
A server CPU: 1 to 2 TFLOPS. A data-centre GPU: over 1000.

title: Fast nodes still wait
for a slow network
caps: Nodes are joined by a LAN, a local-area network.
Each step, every node swaps border weather with its neighbours.
A slow network leaves fast cores waiting for data.

title: Twice the transistors,
about every two years
caps: Moore's law: transistors on a chip double about every two years.
1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Ten years: 32 times as many.
Now chips are hitting limits and falling behind.
So new speed comes from more cores and more nodes.

title: The part that must run
in order stays put
caps: 10 sums must run in order. 100 more can be shared.
On 1 processor: 110 sums in a row.
On 10 processors the 100 split ten ways. The 10 do not.
Time of 20 sums: a speedup of 5.5, not 10.
The sequential part sets the limit.

title: More processors help,
up to a limit
caps: p: the share of time that can be shared. s: its speedup.
90% shareable: 8 processors give 4.7×, 64 give 8.8×.
It can never beat 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10×.
50% shareable: even 32 processors stay below 2×.

title: A costly machine
must never sit idle
caps: Owning it costs admins, support, power and cooling.
A resource manager allocates hardware and schedules the work.
It starts the work on many nodes and monitors it.
Each job waits in a queue that sets the order.

title: Partitions are queues,
most important first
caps: Slurm: Kestrel's resource manager and scheduler.
Partitions: cpu has 6 nodes, gpu has 2. Each is a queue.
The high-priority job takes 4 nodes, the next takes 2.
No nodes left: the third job waits.

title: Submit, check,
run, read the record
caps: sbatch submits job 4021. Nodes are busy, so it waits.
squeue shows it pending, PD. Then it gets n1 to n4.
srun launches a job step: 4 tasks, one per node.
sacct shows the record: completed in 5 h 12 min.
